1: (a) Most candidates understood that a trade union tried to protect workers’ rights. Better responses were able to provide a precise definition. Some answers confused the term with a trade organisation so incorrectly assumed its role was to promote international business. (c) Most candidates were able to identify at least one opportunity with access to a larger market being a popular choice. Better candidates were able to link their answers to the scenario. (d) This question proved challenging to many candidates. Most were able to identify stakeholder groups such as suppliers and the community. Better responses were then able to explain the possible impact on them of CFE’s decision to downsize its workforce. Only the best answers tried to use the context to support the points made. A common mistake was to identify internal stakeholders which the question did not allow. (e) Good knowledge was evident in most responses. Better answers developed points made and used the information from the stem to help make a justified decision about whether reducing the number of workers was the best way for CFE to reduce costs. Weaker answers were characterised by simple statements such as the cost of redundancy or the impact on other workers. These responses did not develop the points to show how or why they might influence CFE’s decision. Evaluation in most responses was simple or not attempted.
2: (a) Most candidates understood that a brand was how a product was recognised. Better candidates were able to provide a precise definition. (b) Well answered by the majority of candidates. (c) Most candidates could identify one advantage with better responses trying to link their answers to the scenario. A common mistake was to repeat the same point for both advantages as the point could only be rewarded once. (d) The concept of issuing shares as a source of finance was not well understood by many candidates. The strongest candidates understood that shares did not need to be repaid but involved the possible loss of control and then explained why these issues were factors that needed to be considered. Few candidates were able to apply their answer to the scenario so application marks were rarely awarded. Instead of development weaker answers repeated the knowledge points. Some incorrectly assumed that the business would have to pay dividends or stated that shares were a quick source of finance. (e) Good knowledge and application was evident in most responses. Better candidates developed points made to explain the possible advantages and disadvantages of each option. Only the best answers offered a supported decision. Some candidates did attempt to make a decision but were not able to offer sufficient reasons to back up the statement made.
3: (a) This question produced a mixture of responses. Many candidates knew that an overdraft was a short term source of finance. Better candidates were able to give a precise definition. A typical error was to confuse the term overdraft with a bank loan. (b) Well answered. (c) The concept of legal controls on marketing was not well understood by many candidates. The strongest candidates understood that such controls would affect how or what was said in advertisements or about its products. Often candidates misinterpreted the question so discussed general marketing issues or other types of legal controls a business might have to consider which was not the question set. A number of candidates did not attempt this question. (d) A large number of candidates were able to clearly explain both an advantage and disadvantage of being a business partnership. Better answers were able to develop points such as sharing responsibilities and profits to show why they were helpful or not for this particular business. (e) Candidates generally understood the different ways to improve cash flow. The best answers addressed the context well and recognised that changing the timing of cash inflows would do little may be a better option. Weaker responses offered simple statements but no development. A number of responses also lacked evaluation.
4: (a) Only the most able candidates were able to give a correct and precise definition. The majority of candidates confused the term with product life cycle - a completely different concept. (b) Most candidates showed good knowledge of flow production. A common mistake was to repeat the same point for both advantages. This could only be awarded once. (c) This question produced a mixture of responses. Many responses identified at least one advantage of using non-financial methods of motivation. Better answers were also able to apply their answers. There were two common mistakes. Some repeated the same answer for both points. Others had the wrong focus and discussed general points which could equally apply to any method of motivation. (d) This question provided challenging for most candidates. It was clear that many did not understand the concept of lean production. Some candidates were able to identify one method but instead of explaining how techniques such as Kaizen and Just In Time could be used to improve efficiency they offered definitions of each term. Few candidates were able to apply their answers to the context. Many responses had the wrong focus and suggested how output could be improved which was not the question set. A number of candidates did not attempt this question. (e) Good knowledge of the advantages and disadvantages of the two types of recruitment was evident in most responses.
